"America Comes Home"

A Speech Advocating Full Isolationist Policy

My fellow Americans,

For over a century, we have been told that America's destiny lies out there — across oceans, in distant deserts, in foreign capitals, in conflicts that have no end and serve no clear purpose for the people of this nation. Tonight, I stand before you to say what millions of Americans feel in their bones but are rarely permitted to say aloud:

It is time to come home.

Not in weakness. Not in retreat. But in wisdom — the very same wisdom our founders possessed when they built this republic.

George Washington, in his farewell address, did not mince words. He warned us — pleaded with us — to steer clear of permanent alliances, of emotional attachments to foreign nations, of the seductive idea that we must be the referee, the policeman, and the banker of the entire world. Thomas Jefferson echoed him: "Peace, commerce, and honest friendship with all nations — entangling alliances with none."

These were not timid men. These were revolutionaries. They defeated an empire. And yet they understood something that we, in our arrogance, have forgotten: A nation that tries to save everyone else will eventually be unable to save itself.

Look around you. Look at this country — really look at it.

Our bridges are crumbling. Our roads are ranked among the worst in the developed world. Our electrical grid is aging, vulnerable, and decades behind what it should be. We have communities in this country — right now, today — where the water is not safe to drink, where hospitals are closing, where schools are failing, where factories sit as hollow monuments to a prosperity we shipped overseas.

And what are we spending? What is the cost of our so-called "global leadership"?

We maintain over 750 military bases in approximately 80 countries. We spend more on defense than the next ten nations combined. We have poured trillions — trillions — into wars in Iraq, Afghanistan, Libya, Syria. Trillions that bought us what, exactly? Stability? Peace? Democracy? Look at those nations today. Then look at our own.

We have spent twenty years and over eight trillion dollars on post-9/11 military operations, according to Brown University's Costs of War Project. Eight trillion dollars. Do you know what eight trillion dollars could build here? That is universal healthcare. That is a modernized infrastructure from coast to coast. That is free public university for every young American for generations. That is the complete elimination of homelessness. That is a national investment in energy independence that would make us untouchable.

Instead, we have thirty-three trillion dollars in national debt, a hollowed-out middle class, a mental health crisis, an opioid epidemic, crumbling rural communities, and veterans — the very people we sent to fight these foreign wars — sleeping under bridges and waiting months for medical care.

Tell me: whose interests are we serving?

They will call me naive. They always do. The foreign policy establishment — the think tanks, the defense contractors, the career diplomats, the pundits — they will say the world needs us. That without American engagement, chaos will reign. That our enemies will fill the vacuum.

Let me address that directly.

First: the world is full of capable, wealthy, advanced nations. Europe has a larger combined economy than we do. Japan, South Korea, Australia — these are prosperous, technologically sophisticated countries. Why are we still subsidizing their defense? Why are American taxpayers footing the bill so that European nations can fund generous social programs while spending a fraction of what we spend on their own security? We are told this is "alliance." I call it dependency — and it weakens them as much as it drains us.

If our allies cannot or will not defend themselves after seventy-five years of American protection, then our protection has not strengthened them. It has made them complacent. A true friend does not carry you forever. A true friend helps you stand on your own.

Second: the argument that we must be everywhere to prevent chaos everywhere is not borne out by our own record. Our interventions have not, by and large, produced the outcomes we were promised. We were told Iraq would become a beacon of democracy. We were told Libya would stabilize after Gaddafi. We were told nation-building in Afghanistan would succeed. The architects of these policies were not evil — many were sincere — but they were wrong. And the price of being wrong was not paid by them. It was paid by American families in small towns across this country who sent their sons and daughters to fight, and by the people in those nations who suffered the consequences of our miscalculations.

How many times must we repeat the same experiment and expect a different result before we call it what it is?

Third — and I want to be very clear about this — disengagement does not mean defenselessness. An isolationist America is not a weak America. It is, in fact, a stronger America. We would maintain the most powerful military in the history of the world. We would defend our borders, our coastlines, our airspace, and our people with overwhelming force. No nation on Earth would dare strike us. Our nuclear deterrent alone guarantees that.

What we would stop doing is deploying that military in every regional dispute, every civil war, every geopolitical chess match that has nothing to do with the safety of the American people. We would stop treating American soldiers as a global resource and start treating them as what they are: our neighbors, our children, our sacred trust.

Now, I want to speak to something deeper. Something that goes beyond budgets and bases.

There is a sickness in a nation that knows more about conflicts ten thousand miles away than it knows about the suffering in its own backyard. There is something profoundly disordered about a political class that will mobilize billions of dollars overnight for a foreign crisis but cannot summon the will to fix the pipes in Flint, Michigan — or Jackson, Mississippi — or the hundred other communities that never made the news.

This is not a question of compassion. I have compassion for people around the world who suffer. But I also have a question that no one in Washington seems willing to answer:

When is it our turn?

When do the people of Appalachia matter as much as the people of Kabul? When do the struggling families in the Rust Belt get the same urgency as a territorial dispute in the South China Sea? When does the single mother working two jobs in Detroit receive the same passionate advocacy that we give to foreign governments?

I am told we are the richest country in the world. Then act like it — for our own people. I am told we are the greatest nation in history. Then prove it — by building a society that reflects that greatness, not by scattering our resources and our blood across every continent.

Let me also say this plainly: the current system is not just ineffective — it is corrupting.

Foreign entanglements don't just cost money. They distort our politics. They create a permanent class of interests — defense contractors, lobbyists, foreign governments — who profit from our engagement and who will always find a reason to keep us involved. President Eisenhower — a five-star general, a man who led the liberation of Europe, hardly a pacifist — warned us about the military-industrial complex. He saw it coming. He told us to be vigilant.

We did not listen.

Today, the defense industry spends hundreds of millions lobbying Congress. Foreign nations spend millions more. And somehow, somehow, the result is always the same: more involvement, more spending, more deployments, more entanglement. The machine feeds itself. And every dollar it consumes is a dollar that did not go to an American school, an American hospital, an American family.

This is not democracy shaping foreign policy. This is foreign policy shaping — and distorting — our democracy.

What would an America that came home look like?

Imagine this:

An America where every cent currently spent maintaining bases in countries that don't want us is redirected into rebuilding our infrastructure — roads, bridges, railways, broadband, the electrical grid. Not over decades. Over years.

An America where we achieve true energy independence, owing nothing to any foreign regime, beholden to no overseas supply chain for our survival.

An America where our manufacturing base is restored — where we make what we need, where our workers have dignified, well-paying jobs, where our supply chains are ours.

An America where our veterans — every single one of them — receive immediate, world-class care, not as a political talking point but as a national obligation.

An America where our borders are secure — not as a slogan, but as a reality — because we have the resources and the focus to manage them properly.

An America where the brilliance of our scientists, our engineers, our entrepreneurs is directed not at building smarter bombs for foreign wars, but at solving the challenges that face us here: clean energy, medical breakthroughs, technological innovation that benefits American families.

An America that trades freely and openly with the world — because isolationism does not mean isolation. We would still trade. We would still have diplomacy. We would still welcome the world's goods and ideas. What we would not do is pledge our blood and treasure to solve the world's unsolvable conflicts.

This is not a fantasy. This is a choice. And it is a choice that every generation of Americans has the right to make.

I know the objections. I respect them. Let me address the most serious.

"What about our moral obligations?"

I feel the weight of that question. I do. But I ask you: do we not have a moral obligation to our own people? Is there not something deeply immoral about a government that neglects its own citizens — that allows poverty, addiction, homelessness, and despair to fester at home — while pouring its wealth into foreign ventures? Charity, true charity, begins with a strong foundation. You cannot pour from an empty cup. We must fill our own cup first — and then, from a position of genuine strength and stability, we can be generous in ways that are sustainable and effective.

"What about China? What about Russia?"

These are serious powers. I do not dismiss them. But our greatest competition with China is not military — it is economic and technological. And we are losing that competition not because we lack aircraft carriers, but because we have failed to invest in our own people, our own education, our own innovation. Every dollar we spend on a base in a country most Americans cannot find on a map is a dollar China is spending on artificial intelligence, on infrastructure, on the industries of the future. We are not going to outcompete China by maintaining a global military empire. We are going to outcompete China by out-building, out-innovating, and out-investing them — and that requires focus, resources, and the political will to put America first. Not as a slogan. As a strategy.

As for Russia — Russia has an economy smaller than Italy's. They are a regional power with nuclear weapons. Our nuclear deterrent checks them. We do not need to be entangled in every border dispute on their periphery to be safe. We need to be strong at home.

"What about global trade and the international order?"

Trade does not require military entanglement. We traded with the world long before we had bases in 80 countries. Commerce is driven by mutual benefit, not by aircraft carriers. The international order we built after World War II served its purpose — it rebuilt Europe, it contained the Soviet Union, it created decades of relative stability. But that order was built for a different world. The Soviet Union is gone. Europe is rebuilt. It is not 1945 anymore. Clinging to a framework built for a vanished world is not wisdom. It is nostalgia. And nostalgia is a luxury we can no longer afford.

I want to close with this.

I love this country. I love it not for what it does abroad, but for what it is — or what it can be — at home. I love the idea of a nation where every child has a genuine shot at a good life. Where communities are strong. Where families can thrive. Where the government serves its people — not the other way around.

That nation is not built by spreading ourselves across the globe. It is built by gathering our strength, our focus, our resources, and our love of country, and directing them inward — toward the land we actually live in, toward the people we actually share this republic with.

For too long, we have been told that patriotism means projecting power. I say patriotism means building a country worthy of the sacrifices our people have already made. I say patriotism means looking an American veteran in the eye and saying: We will never again send you to die for a cause that does not directly protect this nation. I say patriotism means looking at every struggling community in this country and saying: You are not forgotten. You are the priority. You have always been the priority — we just lost our way.

The world will adjust. The world adjusted before America was a superpower, and it will find its balance again. Other nations will step up — because they must. And America, freed from the crushing weight of global obligation, will rise — not as the world's policeman, but as the world's example. A nation so strong, so prosperous, so well-governed, so innovative that others emulate us not because we force them to, but because they want to.

That is American greatness. Not empires. Not bases. Not endless wars. But a republic — strong, free, solvent, and devoted to its own people.

It is time to come home.

It is time to rebuild.

It is time to put America first — not on a bumper sticker, but in our budgets, in our policies, in our priorities, and in our hearts.

Thank you, and God bless the United States of America.

Embracing True Sovereignty: The Imperative for Total American Isolationism

In an era defined by endless wars, ballooning national debt, and the erosion of domestic priorities, the United States stands at a crossroads. For over a century, America has projected its power across the globe, entangling itself in foreign alliances, maintaining a sprawling network of overseas military bases, and meddling in the political and military affairs of distant nations. This interventionist posture, born from the ashes of World War II, has not only failed to secure lasting peace but has actively undermined the nation's prosperity, security, and moral standing. It is time—indeed, it is overdue—for a radical return to the foundational principles of our republic: total isolationism. By withdrawing from all international alliances, closing every overseas military base, and disengaging completely from foreign political and military involvements, the United States can reclaim its sovereignty, redirect its resources inward, and forge a future of unassailable strength and self-reliance.

The historical case for isolationism is irrefutable, rooted in America's own success story. From its founding through the early 20th century, the United States adhered to a policy of splendid isolation, as articulated by George Washington in his Farewell Address: "It is our true policy to steer clear of permanent alliances with any portion of the foreign world." This approach allowed the young nation to focus on westward expansion, industrial growth, and internal development without the drain of foreign entanglements. The Monroe Doctrine further reinforced this stance, warning European powers to stay out of the Western Hemisphere while implicitly committing America to the same restraint abroad. Prosperity followed: by 1914, the U.S. had become the world's leading economic power, unburdened by the imperial overreach that plagued Europe.

Contrast this with the post-World War II era, where America abandoned isolationism for global hegemony. The creation of NATO in 1949, the stationing of troops in Europe and Asia, and interventions from Korea to Vietnam, Iraq, Afghanistan, and beyond have yielded nothing but quagmires. These commitments have cost trillions—estimates for post-9/11 wars alone exceed $8 trillion—and thousands of American lives. Moreover, they have entangled the U.S. in proxy conflicts that serve no clear national interest, from the Cold War's ideological crusades to today's proxy battles in Ukraine and the Middle East. Isolationism is not naivety; it is wisdom learned from history's harsh lessons. By severing these ties, America would avoid the domino effect of alliances that drag it into wars not of its making, echoing the fatal miscalculation that pulled the U.S. into World War I through entangling pacts.

Economically, total isolationism would unleash a renaissance for the American people. The U.S. military budget, currently exceeding $800 billion annually—the highest in the world and more than the next ten countries combined—funds a global empire that America can no longer afford. Overseas bases in places like Germany, Japan, and South Korea cost billions to maintain, siphoning resources that could transform domestic life. Imagine redirecting even half of that expenditure: crumbling infrastructure could be rebuilt with high-speed rail networks rivaling Europe's; underfunded schools could receive world-class funding to cultivate the next generation of innovators; and a universal healthcare system could finally address the inequities that plague millions. The national debt, now over $34 trillion, is a ticking time bomb fueled by endless foreign adventures. Isolationism would slash this burden, fostering fiscal responsibility and economic growth. Trade would continue—America's vast markets ensure that—but without the political strings of alliances like the WTO or IMF, which often disadvantage U.S. workers in favor of globalist agendas. A self-sufficient America, focused on domestic manufacturing and energy independence, would thrive as it did in the isolationist golden age, proving that true wealth comes from within, not from policing the world.

National security, far from being jeopardized by isolationism, would be fortified. The conventional wisdom peddled by interventionists—that overseas bases deter aggression—is a myth perpetuated by the military-industrial complex. In reality, these bases make America a target, breeding resentment and terrorism. The 9/11 attacks were not random; they were blowback from decades of meddling in the Middle East, from supporting dictators to invading sovereign nations. Al-Qaeda's leader, Osama bin Laden, explicitly cited U.S. troops in Saudi Arabia as a casus belli. By closing all 800-plus overseas bases and withdrawing from alliances like NATO, the U.S. would shrink its global footprint, reducing the number of enemies who view America as an imperialist bully. A fortress America, defended by the world's most advanced navy, air force, and missile defenses, would be impregnable. Borders would be secured not through futile nation-building abroad but through robust immigration controls and cyber fortifications at home. Neutral powers like Switzerland and Sweden have thrived for centuries without alliances or bases, relying on deterrence through neutrality and domestic strength. America, with its geographic advantages—oceans on both coasts and friendly neighbors—could do the same, emerging safer and more respected.

Sovereignty itself demands isolationism. International alliances erode American autonomy, subjecting U.S. policy to the whims of foreign governments. NATO's Article 5, for instance, commits the U.S. to defend any member's territory, even if the provocation is dubious—think of Turkey's authoritarian drifts or Europe's internal squabbles. The United Nations, with its endless resolutions and peacekeeping missions, further dilutes U.S. interests, forcing America to foot the bill for a body that often condemns its own actions. Foreign aid, totaling $50 billion yearly, props up corrupt regimes while domestic poverty festers. Disengagement would restore decision-making to the American people and their elected representatives, free from the lobbying of globalist elites. No longer would presidents commit troops based on alliance obligations or vague "humanitarian" pretexts; instead, military action would be reserved for direct threats to the homeland, as the Founders intended. This is not retreat; it is reclamation of the republic's independence, echoing John Quincy Adams's warning that America "goes not abroad in search of monsters to destroy."

Critics will cry that isolationism invites chaos, that adversaries like China or Russia would fill the vacuum. But consider: America's mere existence as a beacon of freedom and innovation deters tyranny more effectively than gunboat diplomacy. Without U.S. meddling, regional powers would resolve their conflicts locally, as they did for millennia before American interventionism upset the balance. The United States should adopt a policy of total strategic independence: complete withdrawal from all permanent international alliances, closure of all overseas military bases, and full disengagement from foreign political and military conflicts.

This is not retreat. It is restoration.

1. Alliances Have Become Liabilities, Not Assets

NATO, and our network of bilateral security treaties with Japan, South Korea, the Philippines, and dozens of other nations, were products of the Cold War. That world no longer exists. Today these alliances function as a one-way security guarantee where America assumes all the risk and all the cost.

Article 5 of NATO obligates American sons and daughters to die for border disputes in the Balkans or the Baltics that have no bearing on American security. Our treaty with Japan could drag us into a war over uninhabited islands in the East China Sea. Our presence in the Middle East makes us a combatant in millennia-old conflicts we cannot resolve.

George Washington warned in his Farewell Address against "permanent, inveterate antipathies against particular nations, and passionate attachments for others." He was right. Every alliance we maintain is a tripwire for a war the American people have not debated, have not voted for, and do not want. A clean break from all alliances restores the power to declare war where the Constitution places it: with Congress, acting solely in defense of the United States.

2. The Overseas Base Empire Bankrupts America and Weakens Our Defense

The United States maintains roughly 750 military installations in over 80 countries. We garrison 60,000 troops in Germany, 55,000 in Japan, and 28,000 in South Korea - countries that are among the wealthiest on earth.

The cost is staggering. Trillions of dollars have been spent building, staffing, and defending this global infrastructure since 1945, not counting the wars it enables. That is money not spent on our own borders, our own infrastructure, our own industrial base, our own debt.

Strategically, these bases do not make us safer. They make us vulnerable. They are fixed targets for missiles, terrorism, and political blackmail. They create a logistical doctrine of power projection that assumes we must fight everywhere, which means we are prepared to fight nowhere decisively. A forward-deployed empire stretches our military thin.

True defense is territorial. A military focused on the defense of the continental United States, Alaska, Hawaii, and our airspace and waters is invincible. A military scattered across Europe, Africa, and Asia is overextended and exhausted. Close the bases, bring the troops home, and rebuild a military whose sole mission is defending the United States.

3. Non-Intervention is the Only Moral and Constitutional Foreign Policy

For 25 years, the interventionist consensus has delivered failure after failure. Iraq, Afghanistan, Libya, Syria, Ukraine - each intervention was sold as vital to U.S. interests, each resulted in dead Americans, hundreds of thousands of dead civilians, trillions wasted, and outcomes far worse than before.

The federal government has no constitutional authority to act as the world's police, to engage in nation-building, or to redistribute American wealth as foreign aid to secure influence. Its duty is to the liberty and welfare of the American people.

Total political disengagement means an end to interfering in foreign elections, an end to funding foreign governments, an end to regime-change wars, and an end to using sanctions and threats as tools to dictate how other peoples govern themselves. Other nations have the right to self-determination, even when we disagree with how they exercise it. We would demand no less for ourselves.

4. Isolationism is Strength, Not Weakness

Critics will call this isolationism as if it were an insult. It is not. It is independence. Economic interdependence can continue through free trade conducted by private citizens and companies, but the American state should no longer be entangled in the political management of the planet.

An isolated America is a richer America, as its capital and talent are reinvested at home. It is a freer America, as the national security state built to justify global interventionism - warrantless surveillance, secret wars, emergency powers - loses its justification. It is a more peaceful America, because a nation that does not intervene is a nation that has few enemies.

The world does not need an American hegemon. It never did. Let Europe defend Europe. Let Asia balance Asia. Let regional powers manage regional problems. The natural geographical security of the United States - two vast oceans and peaceful neighbors - is a strategic gift that most nations in history would have envied. We have squandered that gift for a century in pursuit of empire.

It is time to come home. Withdraw from NATO and all treaties. Close every base on foreign soil. Bring our troops, our dollars, and our future back within our own borders. Let the United States be what it was meant to be: a free, prosperous, and independent Republic, an example to the world, not its master.
